packages.title: ONS territorial/residence/footprint separation QA
facts: ONS identifies three distinct UK GHG accounting bases: territorial, residence and footprint.
Territorial emissions cover emissions occurring within UK borders.
Residence emissions align with National Accounts and UK resident or registered economic activity.
Footprint emissions attribute supply-chain emissions to UK consumption wherever they arise.
Values from the three bases must not be compared as if they share the same boundary or reference year.

packages.title: ONS 2025 territorial versus 2024 residence QA
facts: ONS reports an estimated 367 MtCO2e of UK territorial emissions for 2025.
ONS reports provisionally estimated residence-basis emissions of 478 MtCO2e for 2024.
The territorial and residence figures use different accounting boundaries.
The two headline figures also use different reference years.
The numerical difference must not be interpreted as a one-year change.

packages.title: Defra 2023 direct-household footprint QA
facts: The UK consumption carbon footprint for 2023 is estimated at 699 MtCO2e.
Direct household fossil-fuel emissions were 122 MtCO2e in 2023.
Direct household emissions include private motoring and home heating fossil-fuel use.
Direct household emissions are one component of the wider consumption footprint.
A national household component does not provide a parcel-specific emissions measurement.

packages.title: Defra 2023 import-embedded footprint QA
facts: Imported goods and services contributed 371 MtCO2e to the UK consumption footprint in 2023.
Import-related emissions represented 53% of the UK carbon footprint in 2023.
Import emissions occur in global supply chains rather than necessarily inside UK territory.
Consumption-basis import emissions must not be mixed with territorial source-sector totals.
Imported-emissions shares do not identify emissions at a UK parcel.

packages.title: Defra carbon-footprint revision-method QA
facts: Defra states that previous carbon-footprint years are revised in annual updates.
The 2026 update switches traded-data methodology to FIGARO v2025 from 2010 onward.
Earlier years up to 2009 use EXIOBASE v3.8.3 for trade data in the 2026 update.
A 7 July 2026 correction changed wording about the EU import contribution.
Historical values must therefore retain the release and methodology version used.

packages.title: ONS residence-basis household share QA
facts: ONS estimates 478 MtCO2e of residence-basis UK GHG emissions in 2024.
Households accounted for 25.9% of residence-basis emissions in the 2024 estimate.
The transport industry accounted for 16.3% on the same residence basis.
Industry shares on a residence basis are not territorial source-sector shares.
Residence-basis household emissions cannot be directly assigned to cadastral parcels.

packages.title: ONS direct-energy mix QA
facts: ONS reports fossil fuels as 77.7% of direct UK energy consumption in the 2024 environmental accounts.
ONS reports renewable energy at 15.3% of direct energy consumption on that measure.
Direct energy-use shares are energy metrics rather than GHG-emission shares.
Energy-source shares must retain the Environmental Accounts residence framework.
National energy shares do not prove the fuel mix of a specific property.

packages.title: ONS GHG intensity and GVA QA
facts: ONS reports UK GHG intensity falling from 500 to 140 tonnes CO2e per £1 million GVA between 1990 and 2024.
The reported reduction over that period is 72%.
GHG intensity is an emissions-per-economic-output ratio.
An intensity ratio is not an absolute emissions total.
National economic intensity cannot be used as a parcel emissions value without parcel activity data.

packages.title: ONS quarterly GHG temporal-disaggregation QA
facts: ONS quarterly GHG estimates use a Chow-Lin regression-based temporal disaggregation method.
The dataset is explicitly an estimate rather than direct continuous measurement of every source.
Quarterly editions are identified by reference quarter.
Model-derived quarterly estimates should retain their method and edition.
Quarterly model estimates do not provide parcel-level measurement.

packages.title: Local GHG coverage exclusions QA
facts: DESNZ local GHG statistics cover nationally allocated CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions.
Aviation, shipping and military transport are excluded because there is no obvious basis for local allocation.
Fluorinated gases are excluded because suitable local estimation data are not available.
The exclusions mean local-authority totals are not identical to complete UK territorial totals.
Missing excluded sectors must not be filled with invented local or parcel values.

packages.title: Local GHG uncertainty and LULUCF QA
facts: The local-GHG technical report assesses uncertainty using national-emission and spatial-distribution uncertainty components.
LULUCF uncertainty is excluded from the main sector uncertainty combination because it can dominate local results.
The report gives a UK median local-authority uncertainty of ±4.8% excluding LULUCF.
The UK median becomes ±5.6% when LULUCF is included.
Uncertainty values belong to local-authority estimates and are not parcel-confidence scores.

packages.title: Local GHG minor-road uncertainty QA
facts: The technical report identifies relatively high uncertainty for minor-road emissions.
There are too few direct traffic measurements on minor-road links for detailed modelling everywhere.
Regional traffic flows are used for minor roads where detailed measurements are insufficient.
Average flows and speeds do not capture all temporal variation.
Modelled minor-road emissions must not be presented as measured parcel emissions.

packages.title: Local GHG electricity mapping-quality QA
facts: The local-GHG method uses DESNZ electricity consumption data for spatial allocation.
The technical report states that 97.7% of postcodes were located correctly for industry and commercial electricity.
The uncertainty assessment also allows for estimated MPAN readings.
Electricity consumption mapping is a spatial allocation method rather than direct GHG measurement at every site.
Mapped local-authority electricity emissions require a separate gate before parcel attribution.

packages.title: Large-installation location versus parcel QA
facts: Large industrial installations use point-source information in the local-GHG methodology.
Point-source data can provide stronger location evidence than broad area modelling.
Installation reporting boundaries can differ from cadastral parcel boundaries.
ETS or pollution-inventory installation data do not automatically identify a unique land parcel.
Parcel attribution requires an explicit installation-to-geometry match.

packages.title: DfT zero-emission vehicle tailpipe-definition QA
facts: DfT defines zero-emission vehicles in this series as vehicles reported to emit 0 g CO2 per kilometre from the tailpipe.
The current ZEV categories include battery-electric and fuel-cell electric vehicles.
The definition is a tailpipe criterion.
Zero tailpipe CO2 does not by itself establish zero lifecycle GHG emissions.
Vehicle-type statistics do not provide parcel-specific emissions.

packages.title: DfT vehicle registration versus licensed-stock QA
facts: DfT reports 768,970 vehicles first registered in the UK in 2026 Q1.
Licensed-vehicle stock is a separate measure from first registrations.
Vehicles can leave licensed stock through SORN, scrappage, write-off or export.
Registration flows must not be added to licensed stock as if they were the same measure.
Neither stock nor registration count is a direct GHG emissions measurement.

packages.title: DfT zero-emission car registration-share QA
facts: DfT reports 137,749 zero-emission cars first registered in 2026 Q1.
Zero-emission cars accounted for 21.8% of new car registrations in 2026 Q1.
The comparison share for 2025 Q1 was 20.3%.
A registration share describes market flow rather than distance travelled.
Registration share cannot be converted to emissions without activity and energy data.

packages.title: DfT zero-emission licensed-stock share QA
facts: At the end of March 2026 DfT reported about 2.148 million licensed zero-emission vehicles in the UK.
Zero-emission vehicles represented 5.1% of all licensed vehicles in the headline UK measure.
Licensed-stock share is distinct from new-registration share.
Licensed vehicles can have very different annual mileages.
Licensed-stock share does not establish local or parcel emissions.
